Japanese quail (Coturnix japonica) eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days], a developmental period that is relatively short compared to many other galliform species. Newly emerged chicks exhibit a wet weight at birth of 6.5 grams [Wwb = 6.5 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the species' altricial to semi-precocial developmental strategy. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg itself is recorded at 8.2 grams [Ww0 = 8.2 grams], representing the entire maternally derived investment before embryonic growth commences. This value is closely tied to female body condition and varies modestly across clutches depending on maternal nutrition. During the first days of life, the downy chicks are highly dependent on the hen for thermoregulation and for guidance to food sources, although they begin pecking at crumbled feed almost immediately. The rapid growth trajectory observed in this species is a hallmark of captive-bred populations selected for meat and egg production.

Under the typical thermal conditions of active metabolism in adult Japanese quail, around 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a series of important developmental milestones are achieved within predictable timeframes. Fledging, defined as the achievement of coordinated flight sufficient to escape predators and traverse short distances, occurs at approximately 3 days after hatching [tx = approximately 3 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This extraordinarily rapid onset of flight capability is characteristic of precocial galliforms and allows chicks to follow the hen away from the nest scrape to foraging grounds. Sexual maturation, marked by the first visible signs of gonadal development and the onset of secondary sexual characteristics, is reached at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] in females, while males may mature slightly earlier at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This timing is constrained by the need to complete skeletal growth and accumulate sufficient body reserves before reproductive effort can be initiated.

Body mass trajectories in Japanese quail show pronounced sexual dimorphism as individuals approach adulthood. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the asymptotic body mass attained by fully grown breeding adults, is approximately 250 grams [Wwi = approximately 250 grams]. Males, by contrast, reach a smaller ultimate wet weight of 242 grams [Wwi = 242 grams], a difference that reflects the selective pressures of male-male competition and female investment in egg production. These values are considerably larger than the roughly 100-gram averages reported for wild populations on Avibase, indicating strong artificial selection in domesticated strains. The growth period from hatching to asymptotic mass spans roughly 6 to 8 weeks under ad libitum feeding, with most individuals achieving 90 percent of their adult mass by the time of reproductive maturation. Body condition at the onset of laying is a critical determinant of clutch size and egg quality.

Longevity records for captive Japanese quail indicate a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] when maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a duration that is impressive for a small galliform and reflects the species' relatively slow pace of aging under protected conditions. In wild settings, mortality from predation and environmental stress typically truncates this lifespan considerably, with few individuals surviving beyond two breeding seasons. The first successful breeding event for females occurs relatively late in life compared to the rapid somatic growth, at approximately 928 days after hatching [tR = approximately 928 days after hatching], at an average body temperature of 38.17 °C [T = 38.17 °C]. This delayed onset of reproduction, nearly three times the age at puberty, suggests a strategic allocation of early-life resources toward continued somatic investment and social hierarchy establishment before the energetic demands of egg production are undertaken.

Reproductive output in Japanese quail is considerable, reflecting the species' r-selected life history strategy within a managed captive environment. Females typically produce a clutch of 10 to 14 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 10 to 14 eggs], and under optimal conditions, they can lay as many as 25 to 30 clutches in a single year [F_R_i = 25 to 30 clutches in a single year]. This remarkable frequency is facilitated by short incubation periods and rapid ovarian recovery following each clutch completion. The maximum reproductive rate is thus achieved when sustained at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a temperature that approximates the thermoneutral zone for the species and minimizes the energetic overhead of thermoregulation during laying.
